nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What mismatch is identified in relation to coral populations and climate change?
nodes.answer: The selective pressure imposed by the rapid rate of anthropogenic climate change is mismatched with coral demography, including their growth, reproductive, and recruitment rates.
nodes.paragraph: 2016) with variation sometimes being greater within a single reef than among multiple reef sites (Naugle et al. 2024). There is evidence that corals have already adapted to warming occurring over recent history (Logan et al. 2014; Sully et al. 2019). However, the selective pressure imposed by the rapid rate of anthropogenic climate change is mis- matched with coral demography (growth, reproductive, and recruitment rates) and will likely outpace the ability of many coral populations to fully exploit their adaptive potential on a commensurate timescale (Bay et al. 2017; Matz et al. 2018). Mitigating climate change on a global scale is the only long- term solution to maintaining coral reefs as we know them, but active management strategies utilizing extant thermal tolerance may buy time or help promote genetic rescue in specific areas (DeFilippo et al. 2022; Bay et al. 2017). It is important to characterize the prevalence, limits, and diversity of heat tolerance within coral populations to better predict future outcomes and make decisions about interven- tion strategies.

nodes.question: What are the two significant factors that contribute to biodiversity loss mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Eutrophication and climate change are the two significant factors contributing to biodiversity loss.

Both, eutrophication and climate change, likely play a significant role in biodiversity loss, specifically in the decline of insect diversity and abundance (Nessel et al. 2021; Raven and Wagner 2021). Herbivores comprise particularly interesting organisms to study the consequences of global change, as they are sensi- tive to direct as well as indirect effects, the latter being medi- ated by alterations in host-plant quality or availability (Har - vey et al. 2020; Kuczyk et al. 2021a). For instance, increased temperatures during plant growth may diminish host-plant quality for insect herbivores (Bauerfeind and Fischer 2013; Kuczyk et al. 2021a, b), which may result from increased C:N ratios, concentrations of secondary metabolites, and leaf toughness (Meihls et al. 2012; Block et al. 2019). nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What implications do the findings of this study have regarding biodiversity?
nodes.answer: The findings suggest that the interaction of different global change drivers increases the overall threat to biodiversity, highlighting the need for protection of vulnerable species amid environmental changes.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Biodiversity is currently under strong pressure due to anthropogenic global change. Different drivers of global change may exert direct and indirect effects on biodiversity, and may furthermore interact with one another, but our respective knowledge is still very limited. We investigated indirect and interactive effects of two important drivers of global change, eutrophication and climate change, in replicated low- and high-altitude populations of an insect herbivore, the butterfly Lycaena tityrus, in a laboratory setting. We found local adaptation in developmental traits, with low-altitude populations being adapted to warmer temperatures and longer seasons. Lycaena tityrus responded negatively to agriculturally relevant levels of fertilization of its host plant, showing reduced body mass and prolonged development time. Negative effects were particularly pronounced at warmer temperatures and in high-altitude populations. Our study adds to the increasing knowledge that different drivers of global change may interact and thereby increase the overall level of threat to biodiversity. We suggest that populations inhabiting naturally nutrient-poor environments might be even more vulnerable to agricultural intensification than others, potentially applicable to many species. These findings may have important implications for protecting numerous vulnerable species in the face of rapid environmental change.

nodes.answer: The ecological drivers indicated to have an interactive effect on biodiversity loss are eutrophication and climate change.
nodes.paragraph: We predict that (1) cold-adapted high-altitude popula- tions of L. tityrus, which are not (yet) exposed to high levels of eutrophication, are more sensitive to host plant fertiliza- tion than low-altitude populations, and that (2) detrimental effects of fertilization are more pronounced at higher ambi- ent temperatures, indicating an interactive effect between two important drivers of biodiversity loss, eutrophication and climate change. Materials and methods Study organism Lycaena tityrus (Poda 1761) is a widespread, temperate- zone butterfly ranging from Spain throughout large parts of central and southern Europe to western Asia (Ebert and Rennwald 1991; Br u et al. 2013). In most parts of its range, it has 2 3 generations per year (Ebert and Rennwald 1991; Tolman and Lewington 2008). Two subspecies are recog- nized in central Europe, the widespread nominate form L. tityrus tityrus (Poda 1761) and the alpine subspecies L. tityrus subalpinus (Speyer 1851). The latter is confined to the higher altitudes of the European Alps and some other mountain ranges, where it has only one generation per year (Tolman and Lewington 2008).

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How are marine ecosystems being affected by biodiversity loss?
nodes.answer: Modified marine ecosystems are experiencing accelerating species loss, which has largely unknown consequences.
nodes.paragraph: 89 Vol:. (1234567890) Keywords Biological invasions Biosecurity Risk assessment Spatial model Invasion Relative Risk Index MPA Introduction Biodiversity is a term that refers to the variety of life on Earth at all levels, from genes to ecosystems, and can also be used to comprehend processes that sustain life (Swingland 2013). Throughout human history, species have become extinct, and the degradation of ecosystems is likely to accelerate further in the com- ing years (Johnson et al. 2017). Earth S biodiversity is facing an unprecedented crisis, with ecosystems dete- riorating alarmingly due to several sorts of pollution, land-use change (including biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and fragmentation), climate change, and the introduction of non-indigenous species (NIS) (Gaston et al. 2023). The ocean is no exception, with modified marine ecosystems experiencing accelerat- ing species loss with largely unknown consequences (Boris Worm et al. 2006; Nagelkerken and Connell 2022). In this context, global initiatives, such as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Frame- work (GBF), have been established to recognise the urgency of these circumstances.

nodes.question: What is the percentage decline in freshwater biodiversity in the Anthropocene compared to terrestrial and marine environments?
nodes.answer: Freshwater biodiversity has experienced a decline of 76%, while terrestrial and marine environments have seen a decline of 39%.
nodes.paragraph: Indeed, the fresh- water biodiversity loss in the Anthropocene is already pervasive in all taxonomic groups (Reid et al., 2019; Rivaes et al., 2021; Tickner et al., 2020), which experienced a more rapid decline (76%) compared to terrestrial and marine environments (39%) (McLellan et al., 2014). According to the most recent report by Su et al. (2021), anthropogenic activi- ties severely affect fish biodiversity in more than half of the 2,456 river basins worldwide. In Southeast Asia (SEA), freshwater environments play critical socioeconomic and cul- tural roles and host global hotspots of biodiversity and endemism, yet remain among the most threatened in the world (Coleman et al., 2019; Hughes, 2017; Sodhi et al., 2009). The freshwater biota in SEA also received less attention and investments compared to their terrestrial, marine, or temperate counterparts (Coleman et al., 2019; Tydecks et al., 2018), particularly in the Philippines (Magbanua et al., 2017; Papa & Briones, 2017; van der Ploeg et al., 2017).

nodes.answer: If warming is not limited to 1.5°C, climate change is likely to become the dominant cause of biodiversity loss in the coming decades, driving mass mortality events and extinctions of entire species.

Some of the most carbon-rich mangroves are found on the Pacific coast of Colombia - these exceed 50m in height ²5. In addition, mangroves help climate change adaptation, as their tangled above-ground roots are a buffer to waves 26 and trap sediments, allowing some mangroves to increase their surfaces and keep pace with sea-level rise ²7. Despite their importance, mangroves continue to be deforested by aquaculture, agriculture and coastal development, at current rates of 0.13% per year28 Many mangroves are also degraded by overexploitation and pollution, alongside natural stressors such as storms and coastal erosion. Mangrove loss represents the loss of habitat for biodiversity and the loss of ecosystem services for coastal communities, and in some locations it can mean the loss of the very land where coastal communities live. For instance, 137km2 of the Sundarbans mangrove forest have been eroded since 198529, reducing land and ecosystem services for many of the 10 million people who live there. Encouragingly, mangrove deforestation has reduced dramatically since the 1980s 30 and we now have plausible scenarios where the global mangrove area may stabilise or even increase by 2070 31.

nodes.question: What is the main threat to global biodiversity mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Climate change is the most significant threat to global biodiversity.
nodes.paragraph: Predicting habitat suitability of Illicium griffithii under climate change scenarios using an ensemble modeling approach Anubhav Bhuyan1, Amal Bawri2, Bhrigu Prasad Saikia3, Shilpa Baidya1, Suhasini Hazarika1, Bijay Thakur1, Vivek Chetry4, Bidya Sagar Deka1, Pangkhi Bharali4, Amit Prakash1, Kuladip Sarma5 & Ashalata Devi1 Climate change is the most significant threat to global biodiversity , risking extinction for many species due to their limited adaptability to rapidly changing environmental conditions, such as temperature, precipitation, and other climate variables. Illicium griffithii , an endangered tree with ecological and medicinal value, remains understudied, particularly in Arunachal Pradesh. The aim of the study is to identify key environmental variables influencing the current distribution of I. griffithii and to predict the potential distribution under current and future climatic scenarios ( SSP245 and SSP585). We used an ensemble modeling approach that integrates five species distribution models ( SDMs). After multicollinearity test, we utilized fifteen environmental variables including bioclimatic variables, soil properties, topographical variables, and evapotranspiration to predict the potential distribution of I. griffithii . The study revealed that the current distribution is predominantly influenced by isothermality, nitrogen content at 0 5 cm depth, clay content at 0 5 cm depth, and seasonality of precipitation, with a total contribution rate of 42.6%.
